doc.title: Dick Sherman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Growing up with radio and the pop hits of the fifties
summary: Radio and disc jockeys fed his jazz love; he found pop hits like Cry okay but not comparable to jazz.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Was it a big part of your hearing music when you grew up?

Yes it was. Remember, it was before television. Television didn’t appear in my life until 1952 around the time of the Eisenhower election. And we got a T.V. set over in the DU House and we were really excited. But it was radio. And a few disc jockeys were famous for playing jazz and I would tune in all the time to that. And what you see is the results.

Well I had thrown a few song names at Phil, like the stuff that was getting top 10 airplay in the fifties and you had things, even a Leroy Anderson song, “Blue Tango,” “How High the Moon” by Les Paul.
So there was that going on but then you had Johnny Ray doing “Cry.” Did those kinds of things, Dean Martin, Perry Como, did they appeal to you?
Sure, they were okay. But I didn’t really love them the way I love jazz.
Right. And you couldn’t play them, I mean it would be that—
Oh no, can you imagine trying to play “Cry?” It would make you cry.
